newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - S.African poultry industry cries foul over imports.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - S.African poultry industry cries foul over imports.

text.p: South Africa's government is trying to balance the interests of consumers seeking low prices and a struggling poultry industry demanding higher tariffs.
Local poultry producers say cheap imports, mainly from the United States, and feared sharp increases in the cost of feed, could drive many to the wall.

Late last year the South African Poultry Association (SAPA) asked the Board on Tariffs and Trade to raise duties to 64 percent from 27 percent to stem imports. The board will send recommendations to Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom, who has frequently expressed support for free trade.

The SAPA application has been opposed by the Association of Meat Importers and Exporters, whose chairman Piet de Wet recently commented: "Protection is immediately considered the moment the going gets tough."
POLITICIANS GET INVOLVED
The opposition Inkatha Freedom Party introduced a new element this month when its farm affairs spokesman Jurie Mentz told Hanekom small black farmers needed protection from U.S. corporate giants.

"Small farmers...in the rural areas are now producing poultry for sale but they are faced with American poultry being brought into the country at 50 percent what it costs to produce them," Mentz told the minister.
He said U.S. imports were hobbling efforts by black producers to move from self-sufficiency to commercial scale operations.
Hanekom responded that tariffs would be used to prevent genuine dumping, but added: "We cannot be artificially protecting industries that cannot be competitive."
Hanekom, whose African National Congress is committed to black empowerment, said he had to balance the interests of producers and consumers.
He has previously tried to dismiss fears that recent agreements with the United States on scrapping non-tariff barriers to farm trade would cause a flood of U.S. chicken imports.
But a meeting between Hanekom and his U.S. counterpart Dan Glickman in Cape Town in February to discuss increased trade did little to soothe poultry industry concerns.
Glickman said trade in farm goods between the two countries had grown 30 percent since 1994, when apartheid was scrapped and trade sanctions were removed.
"There is a great potential for agricultural trade, given the size of our countries. The whole idea is to increase that," he said.
PRODUCERS' FEARS REMAIN
Comments such as these continue to worry poultry producers, in spite of Hanekom's assurances.
"We are being threatened by very cheap imports and the potential of the maize price remaining high," Zac Coetzee, SAPA's chief, told Reuters.

A dry spell in February has raised concerns that this year's maize crop will be well below that of last year. Yellow maize is the major constituent of chicken feed which accounts for around 70 percent of producers' costs.
County Fair, one of the country's top eight chicken producers, said the government was obliged to protect the industry.

"In the countries exporting chicken to South Africa the broiler industries are subsidised in more than one way, whereas in South Africa no financial support exists," said County Fair general manager Barnus Baard.
"We are not playing on a level playing field in comparison to producers in countries like the United States."
ANALYSTS DIVIDED
Industry analysts are divided on the issue.

Stuart Thompson, an analyst at ING Barings, said the most decisive factor in the industry's fortunes this year was whether Rainbow Chicken Ltd, the biggest producer, will cut back on the quantities it offloaded on the market in 1996.
"I have a funny feeling that Rainbow are going to start worrying more about profits than pure turnover and that tends to be good for the other producers," Thompson said.
But another analyst, who asked not to be identified, said higher tariffs might be the only lifebelt for the industry.
"Government really has to take a position on whether they want a poultry industry or not," the analyst said. "With the pricing of maize and imports, we just can't compete."
